title: What is a stored procedure, its benefits, and types (with input/output params)?
shortTitle: Stored Procedures — Benefits and Types (Input/Output Parameters)

s1_definition.profdef: A stored procedure is a named, precompiled block of SQL and procedural logic stored in the database and invoked by name, optionally with parameters. Parameters come in three directions — IN (input, passed in), OUT (output, returned), and INOUT (both) — and procedures may also return a status. Benefits include performance (precompiled, fewer round trips), security (grant execute without table access, and parameterization resists injection), reusability, encapsulation of business logic near the data, and reduced network traffic.
s1_definition.analogy: A stored procedure is like a standard operating procedure kept inside National Bank of India's back office. Instead of a clerk sending ten separate instructions over the phone to move money, they call one named procedure, "TransferFunds," hand it the account numbers and amount (the IN parameters), and it does all the steps inside the vault and hands back a success flag and the new balance (the OUT parameters). The procedure lives where the money is, so it is fast, consistent, and the clerk never needs direct access to the vault's drawers.
s1_definition.oneliner: A stored procedure is named, precompiled SQL logic living in the database, called with IN/OUT/INOUT parameters, giving performance, security, reuse, and encapsulation near the data.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A stored procedure is a named, precompiled block of SQL and procedural logic stored in the database and invoked by name, optionally with parameters. Parameters come in three directions — IN (input, passed in), OUT (output, returned), and INOUT (both) — and procedures may also return a status. Benefits include performance (precompiled, fewer round trips), security (grant execute without table access, and parameterization resists injection), reusability, encapsulation of business logic near the data, and reduced network traffic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A stored procedure is like a standard operating procedure kept inside National Bank of India's back office. Instead of a clerk sending ten separate instructions over the phone to move money, they call one named procedure, "TransferFunds," hand it the account numbers and amount (the IN parameters), and it does all the steps inside the vault and hands back a success flag and the new balance (the OUT parameters). The procedure lives where the money is, so it is fast, consistent, and the clerk never needs direct access to the vault's drawers.

**One line to remember:** A stored procedure is named, precompiled SQL logic living in the database, called with IN/OUT/INOUT parameters, giving performance, security, reuse, and encapsulation near the data.

sections.s2_technical:
A stored procedure is created with `CREATE PROCEDURE name(params) ...` and holds a body written in the engine's procedural language — PL/SQL in Oracle, PL/pgSQL in PostgreSQL, T-SQL in SQL Server, or SQL/PSM in MySQL. The database parses and compiles it once and caches an execution plan, so repeated calls skip reparsing. You invoke it with `CALL name(args)` or `EXEC name args`. Because the logic runs inside the database engine, a multi-step operation that would otherwise require many client-server round trips happens in a single call close to the data.

Parameters have three modes. An IN parameter passes a value into the procedure and is read-only inside it; this is the default. An OUT parameter is written by the procedure and read by the caller after it returns, used to hand back a computed result or a status. An INOUT parameter does both — the caller passes an initial value that the procedure can read and then overwrite. Many engines also allow a procedure to return a result set or, for functions specifically, a return value; the distinction is that functions return a value and can be used inside expressions, while procedures perform actions and communicate through OUT parameters and status.

The benefits make procedures attractive for certain tasks. Performance comes from precompilation, cached plans, and fewer round trips — a nightly batch that touches millions of rows runs far faster executed server-side than row-by-row from the application. Security comes from granting `EXECUTE` on the procedure while denying direct table access, so users can run a vetted operation without touching base tables, and because parameters are bound, procedures naturally resist SQL injection. Reusability and consistency come from centralizing a business rule so every caller applies it identically. Encapsulation keeps complex, data-intensive logic next to the data. The senior nuances to mention are the trade-offs: stored procedures scatter business logic across the database and the application, are harder to version-control and unit-test than application code, create vendor lock-in through engine-specific languages, and can complicate horizontal scaling — so modern teams often keep heavy set-based data operations in procedures while keeping general business logic in the application layer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's fund-transfer operation involves several steps: validate the source balance, debit the source, credit the target, and record an audit row. Doing this from the application meant multiple round trips and risked partial updates. The team encapsulated it in a `transfer_funds` stored procedure taking IN parameters (from account, to account, amount) and OUT parameters (status and resulting source balance), running atomically in the database.

Our mini-project simulates a stored-procedure engine: a `StoredProcedure` abstraction with typed IN/OUT parameters and a `transfer_funds` implementation that validates, debits, credits, and sets OUT status and new balance — demonstrating parameter modes, encapsulation, and a returned status, exactly as the three parameter directions work in a real engine.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts, A100 with fifty thousand and A200 with two thousand, held in the database.

Step 1 — The caller invokes the procedure with three IN parameters: transfer fifteen thousand from A100 to A200. These are read-only inside the procedure.

Step 2 — Inside the procedure the encapsulated logic validates both accounts exist and that A100 has enough funds, then debits A100 and credits A200 — all server-side in one call, not multiple round trips.

Step 3 — The procedure writes two OUT parameters: a status of SUCCESS and the new source balance of thirty-five thousand. The caller reads these after the call returns.

Step 4 — A second call attempts to move an impossible amount from A200. The validation fails, no balances change, and the procedure returns an OUT status of FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, demonstrating how status is communicated through an OUT parameter rather than a thrown exception.

Step 5 — The final balances show only the first, valid transfer took effect, proving the procedure encapsulated the whole operation and reported outcomes through its parameters.

Final output:

```text
Call 1: {p_status=SUCCESS, p_new_from_balance=35000.0}
Call 2: {p_status=FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS, p_new_from_balance=2000.0}
Final balances: {A100=35000.0, A200=17000.0}
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  caller ──CALL transfer_funds(IN from,to,amount; OUT status,newBal)──▶ DB engine
                                                                           │
                              ┌────────────── precompiled proc body ───────┘
                              ▼
   IN p_from,p_to,p_amount ─▶ validate ─▶ debit source ─▶ credit target ─▶ set OUT
                                                                           │
  caller ◀── OUT p_status, OUT p_new_from_balance ─────────────────────────┘
   (one round trip, logic lives in DB, EXECUTE grant only — no table access)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Stored Procedure Encapsulation ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  CALL (1 round trip)  ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ App / batch  │ ────────────────────▶ │ transfer_funds proc   │
  │ (EXECUTE)    │  IN args / OUT results│ precompiled, cached    │
  └──────────────┘                       └───────────────────────┘
        ▲ status + new balance                     │ reads/writes
        └───────────────────────────────           ▼
                                           ┌──────────────┐
                                           │ accounts tbl │  (no direct grant)
                                           └──────────────┘
  Benefits: perf (precompiled, fewer trips) • security (EXECUTE only, bound params)
            • reuse • encapsulation near data   Params: IN / OUT / INOUT
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Procedure & Parameter Modes ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Command: a procedure is a named, parameterized action             │
  │ Context Object: ProcContext carries IN/OUT params                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: proc does one operation (transfer); context carries params    │
  │ O: new proc = new class, caller pattern unchanged                │
  │ D: caller depends on CALL contract, not internals                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Parameter modes ──
  IN    : caller → proc (read-only inside)      [default]
  OUT   : proc → caller (proc writes, caller reads after)
  INOUT : both (caller seeds, proc overwrites)
  also  : RETURN status / result set; FUNCTION returns a value in expressions

  ── Engine languages ── Oracle PL/SQL | PG PL/pgSQL | SQL Server T-SQL | MySQL SQL/PSM

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → setIn(from,to,amount); call(ctx)   [IN params]
  3.       → validate → debit → credit       [encapsulated, atomic]
  4.       → setOut(status,newBalance)        [OUT params]
  5.   → read ctx.outputs()                   [status back to caller]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A stored procedure is a named, precompiled block of SQL and procedural logic that lives inside the database and is invoked by name, optionally with parameters, written in the engine's procedural language — PL/SQL in Oracle, PL/pgSQL in PostgreSQL, T-SQL in SQL Server. The database compiles it once and caches a plan, so repeated calls skip reparsing and a multi-step operation runs in a single server-side call instead of many client-server round trips. Parameters come in three modes: an IN parameter passes a value in and is read-only inside the procedure, an OUT parameter is written by the procedure and read by the caller after it returns, and an INOUT parameter does both, while procedures can also communicate a status or a result set. The distinction from a function is that a function returns a value usable inside an expression, whereas a procedure performs an action and reports through OUT parameters and status.

The benefits I state are performance from precompilation, cached plans, and fewer round trips, which is why a nightly batch over millions of rows runs far faster server-side; security from granting `EXECUTE` on the procedure while denying direct table access and from bound parameters that resist SQL injection; reusability and consistency from centralizing a business rule so every caller applies it identically; and encapsulation that keeps data-intensive logic next to the data. At the National Bank of India we encapsulated fund transfers in a `transfer_funds` procedure that took the source account, target account, and amount as IN parameters and returned a status and the new source balance as OUT parameters, validating, debiting, crediting, and auditing atomically in one call instead of several round trips that risked partial updates. The senior nuances I always add are the trade-offs: procedures scatter business logic between the database and the application, are harder to version-control and unit-test, create vendor lock-in through engine-specific languages, and can complicate scaling, so I keep heavy set-based data operations in procedures and general business logic in the application. The line I always state is that a stored procedure is named, precompiled SQL logic in the database, called with IN, OUT, and INOUT parameters, giving performance, security, reuse, and encapsulation near the data.
